title: Wehrlein passes Wittmann late to win Moscow Race 1
dek: Pascal Wehrlein started second, passed pole-sitter Marco Wittmann with about four minutes left and won by 1.853 seconds to retake the points lead after Ekström and Glock collided.

chapters.title: A new stand-in and a title fight in Russia
text: The DTM arrived at Moscow Raceway for the sixth weekend of 2015, the first season in which every round was split into a Saturday sprint and a longer Sunday race. Saturday's race was the eleventh of 18 on the calendar, and Mattias Ekström came to Russia leading the championship for Audi on 111 points, 13 clear of Edoardo Mortara on 98. Pascal Wehrlein was third on 94 and Jamie Green fourth on 81, so a good Saturday could reshuffle the top of the table.

Marco Wittmann arrived as reigning champion for BMW but outside the top six of the standings, and he had not started a single race from pole position in 2015. There was also a new face in the Audi camp: Antonio Giovinazzi made his DTM debut for Phoenix, standing in for Timo Scheider for the weekend.

Friday's opening practice was led by Wittmann, with Ekström and Mortara close behind and Audis and BMWs filling almost the whole top ten. Daniel Juncadella was the best of the Mercedes drivers in tenth. Saturday's second practice began on a damp track that dried out completely before qualifying, so every car could start the session on dry tyres.

chapters.title: Wittmann takes his first pole of the season
text: Wittmann answered with a 1m28.810s lap in the 20-minute session, set with just under 30 seconds left on the clock. He said the first run had been good but not clean, and that a small change to tyre pressures for the second set made the difference. It was the first pole of his title defence.

Wehrlein improved after the chequered flag to take second, 0.169 seconds behind in his Mercedes. He said he was happy with the result, having expected Mercedes to be a little quicker around the lap. Green put his Audi third on 1m28.985s, only 0.006 seconds behind Wehrlein, which gave all three manufacturers a driver in the top three. Timo Glock had been fastest as the final runs began with four minutes remaining but could not improve on 1m29.003s and ended up fourth. Tom Blomqvist took fifth, the best qualifying result of his rookie DTM career, ahead of Ekström in sixth and Bruno Spengler in seventh, so BMW had four cars in the top seven.

Miguel Molina, Juncadella and Nico Müller completed the top ten. Mortara qualified only twelfth, a row ahead of Paul di Resta in 13th and Mike Rockenfeller in 14th. Giovinazzi was 19th on debut, a solid first qualifying that left him ahead of Gary Paffett's Mercedes in 20th, while Robert Wickens was 22nd and Christian Vietoris last of the 24 runners.

chapters.title: A Turn 1 crash brings out the safety car
text: Wittmann won the start from Wehrlein and Green, while Blomqvist, who started fifth, was slow away and lost places. At Turn 1 Miguel Molina and Vietoris collided and both cars were out on the spot. Vietoris's Mercedes caught fire at the front and he put the flames out himself. The safety car was called and the race stayed neutralised for the first six laps.

Behind the pace car Wittmann led Wehrlein, Green, Glock, Ekström and Spengler. The early chaos also caught di Resta: Rockenfeller made contact with the Mercedes and turned it around, an incident the stewards said they would study after the race. Di Resta recovered to finish 14th. The restart came at the end of lap 6, and Wittmann held his lead into lap 7 with no change in the order behind him.

chapters.title: Ekström and Glock go off together
text: DRS was enabled from lap 10, and Wehrlein immediately started to lean on Wittmann, while Ekström pressed Glock for fourth. On lap 11 the Audi driver went for the inside at Turn 7 and the two cars touched as they turned in. Both slid into the barriers and both were out, which neutralised the race for a second time, until the green flag on lap 14.

Glock said the move came as a surprise and that he had not expected such aggression there. Ekström's version was that he was already alongside and expected to be given room. The stewards blamed the Swede and gave him a three-place grid penalty for Sunday. It ended his race with no points, and with Wehrlein heading for the win it cost him the lead in the championship. Adrien Tambay, running at the back, also stopped at the pits and retired later in the race.

chapters.title: Wehrlein finds a way past in the final minutes
text: After the restart Wittmann led a four-car train of Wehrlein, Green and Spengler, with Juncadella, Blomqvist, Mortara and Müller behind. Wehrlein was within four tenths of the leader on lap 17, and the top four were inside a second on lap 20. With DRS he looked around the outside at the last corner on two consecutive laps without success. Then, with about four minutes to go, he switched to the inside, made the pass stick and pulled away to win by 1.853 seconds.

Wittmann held off Green for second, but on the final lap Spengler passed Green at the last corner to take third, 2.536 seconds behind the winner, and put two BMWs on the podium. Green was fourth, just ahead of Juncadella, with Mortara sixth. Paffett was the race's big mover, climbing from 20th on the grid to seventh, ahead of Blomqvist, Müller and Rockenfeller.

Wittmann said that once Wehrlein began to attack he knew he had no answer, and that even with DRS after being passed he could not keep up. The result gave Wehrlein his second win of 2015 and the championship lead on 119 points, eight ahead of Ekström on 111. Mortara was third on 106 and Green fourth on 93.

facts.v: Pascal Wehrlein won in 41:56.506 over 24 laps, 1.853 seconds ahead of Marco Wittmann, and moved to the top of the standings on 119 points.

facts.v: Wittmann's 1m28.810s was 0.169 seconds faster than Wehrlein, and Jamie Green was third on 1m28.985s.

Ekström was judged at fault for the clash with Glock and given a three-place grid penalty for Sunday's race.
